summary: Describes an LDAP extension that clients can use to ask for all operational attributes to be returned. LDAP previously could request all user attributes but not all operational attributes. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory usually shows only the regular facts about someone. This adds a magic word that also asks for the behind-the-scenes facts the system keeps about the entry.

questions: how to request operational attributes in ldap
what is the ldap plus sign
how to discover ldap operational attributes
subtitle: Requesting all operational attributes in LDAP directory searches.

tldr.problem: LDAP clients could request all user attributes with a wildcard, but there was no standard way to request all operational attributes (system-managed attributes like modification timestamps).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3673 adds a simple extension to LDAPv3: using the plus sign (+) in the attributes list of a search request asks the server to return all operational attributes, following the same pattern used in the X.500 standard.
tldr.outcome: LDAP clients can now discover and retrieve all operational attributes on a directory entry using existing LDAP APIs and clients without modification.

today: RFC 3673 is a Proposed Standard that extends LDAP version 3 by allowing clients to request all operational attributes using the plus sign syntax. The feature has been widely implemented in modern LDAP servers and clients for discovering system-maintained attributes in directory entries.

sections.title: LDAP Attributes: User and Operational
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is used to query directory services. LDAP distinguishes between two types of attributes: user attributes (the information someone actively enters about a directory entry, like a name or email address) and operational attributes (system-managed metadata like timestamps for creation, modification, and last access).

Before RFC 3673, LDAP clients could request all user attributes using a wildcard, but no standard mechanism existed to request all operational attributes at once, making it difficult to discover what operational attributes an entry contained.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone directory has names and phone numbers (user data). But behind the scenes, it also keeps track of when the listing was created and last changed (operational data). There was no easy way to ask for all the behind-the-scenes information.

sections.title: The Plus Sign Extension
sections.content:
RFC 3673 extends LDAP by defining a simple syntax: when a client includes the plus sign character (+, ASCII 43) in the list of requested attributes in a search request, the server returns all operational attributes in the response. This follows the same mechanism already used in X.500 directories.

The extension is designed for use with existing LDAP clients and APIs without requiring any modifications. Servers that do not support this feature simply treat the plus sign as an unrecognized attribute and ignore it, maintaining backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for attributes by name, or put a + sign to say "give me all the behind-the-scenes stuff."

sections.title: Limitations and Interoperability
sections.content:
Clients should note that results may not include all requested attributes due to access controls or other server restrictions. Some operational attributes may be expensive to compute or return, so servers may only return them when explicitly requested by name, even when the plus sign is present.

Servers supporting this feature SHOULD advertise support by publishing a specific Object Identifier (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.1) in the root DSE. The mechanism requires no modification of existing LDAP APIs, making it immediately available in all existing LDAP clients and libraries.
sections.plainLanguage: The server might not return everything due to permissions or performance reasons. Modern LDAP tools automatically understand the + sign without needing updates.
